lessons.hook: In 1900, nearly four in ten American cars were electric, and a century later we are still treating electric mobility as a novelty. The reason they disappeared has less to do with batteries than you might think.

quiz.explanation: The starter eliminated the petrol car's biggest drawback, which had been the electric car's strongest selling point.
options: It made petrol engines more fuel-efficient
It removed the dangerous, tiring hand-cranking that had favoured electric cars
It allowed petrol cars to be recharged
It made petrol cars quieter than electric ones
quiz.question: Why did the electric starter matter so much for petrol cars?

quiz.explanation: Assembly-line production cut car prices while discoveries such as Spindletop made fuel plentiful and cheap.

A ban on electric vehicles in cities

options: Hardware efficiency matters more than user experience
Removing friction from the whole charging experience can drive adoption
Rural areas should be the first market

sections.body:
In 1900, if you had stood on a busy street in New York, you would have been just as likely to see a car gliding along on batteries as one chugging along on petrol. Of the roughly 4,200 cars built in the United States that year, about 38 percent were electric, 40 percent were steam-powered and only 22 percent ran on gasoline. Electric cars were quiet, clean and needed no skill to start. In 1899 a Belgian electric car called La Jamais Contente had even become the first road vehicle to exceed 100 km/h.

Yet within about two decades the electric car had all but vanished. The popular story blames a single villain, but the truth is a chain of small shifts that reinforced one another. That is what makes the episode so instructive: nobody ever decided that electric would lose.
sections.heading: The forgotten head start

sections.body:
Start with the humble crank. Early petrol engines had to be started by hand, by swinging a heavy metal handle at the front of the car. If the engine backfired, the handle could kick back violently, and broken wrists and forearms were common enough to earn their own nickname: the chauffeur's fracture. Beyond the injuries, cranking a cold engine on a winter morning was a real ordeal, which is exactly why electric cars were marketed to doctors, city dwellers and many women drivers.

In 1911 Charles Kettering, working at Delco, developed a compact electric starter motor, and Cadillac fitted it to its 1912 models. Ironically, it was electricity that rescued the combustion engine. Overnight, the electric car's strongest selling point, 'no cranking, just go', became table stakes for everybody. A small motor and battery, an engineer's answer to a usability problem, had removed the petrol car's biggest handicap.
sections.heading: The arm-breaking problem

sections.body:
Then came the economics. Ford's Model T arrived in 1908, and once it was built on a moving assembly line from 1913, its price kept falling, eventually dropping below $300 in the mid-1920s. A typical electric roadster of 1912 cost around $1,750, roughly three times as much as a Model T. Heavy lead-acid batteries were expensive to build and to replace, so the electric car could not follow that price curve.

Fuel supply moved in the opposite direction. The gusher at Spindletop, Texas, in 1901 and the oil fields that followed made gasoline abundant and cheap, and you could buy it almost anywhere in a can. Electric cars were excellent for city errands of 50 to 80 km, but as roads improved and people wanted to travel between towns, the limited range became a serious weakness. In rural America, where most farms had no grid connection until well into the 1930s, an electric car simply could not be recharged.
sections.heading: Cheap oil and a cheaper car

sections.body: The deeper lesson is about feedback loops. Each advantage for petrol made the next one easier: more buyers meant bigger factories, lower prices, more filling stations and more mechanics, which in turn attracted still more buyers. Electric cars, serving a small niche, never crossed the threshold where that cycle could start. Detroit Electric kept building cars until 1939, but as a boutique brand for a loyal few. Today we would call this a network effect, and it explains why the technically elegant option does not always win. The option that is easiest to live with, at scale, usually does.
sections.heading: A feedback loop nobody planned

sections.body:
For anyone building charging software, the parallels are hard to miss. Drivers do not judge an EV by its kilowatt-hours; they judge the whole experience: finding a free charger, starting a session, paying, and trusting that it will actually work. Kettering's starter did not improve the engine at all. It removed friction. Reliable uptime, transparent pricing, roaming and plug-and-charge are today's starter motor.

So when you prioritise a backlog, remember that adoption often hinges on removing one stubborn annoyance rather than on a technical breakthrough. Ask not 'what is the most advanced feature we could add?' but 'what is our version of the hand crank?'
sections.heading: What it means for your roadmap

lessons.takeaway: Electric cars did not lose because the technology failed, but because petrol removed its biggest annoyance, got cheaper, and then fed on its own growth. Removing friction often matters more than adding features.
lessons.title: When Electric Cars Ruled the Road

vocab.definition: strengthened each other through mutual effect, so that each factor made the others more powerful
vocab.example: Poor documentation and rushed releases reinforced one another until the team was drowning in support tickets.

vocab.definition: a very unpleasant or painful experience that is hard to endure
vocab.example: Finding a working public charger on the motorway was an ordeal for the first EV owners.

vocab.definition: the minimum requirement needed to compete in a market; a feature customers simply expect
vocab.example: Real-time availability maps are table stakes for any charging app today.
vocab.pl: absolutne minimum, podstawowy wymóg wejścia do gry

vocab.definition: a small, specialised segment of a market
vocab.example: The startup found its niche by serving small delivery fleets that the big vendors ignored.

vocab.definition: anything that makes a process slower, harder or more annoying for users
vocab.example: Asking drivers to create an account before charging adds needless friction.

vocab.definition: depends entirely on a single factor or condition
vocab.example: The success of the pilot hinges on whether the chargers stay online during the first month.
